prompt: Can you make me a landing page for Tidewick, a small company that sells roasted seaweed snacks? A headline, a short line under it, three little product cards (Sea Salt, Chili Lime, Toasted Sesame) and a Shop now button. We don't have brand colors yet. I want it to feel fresh but not like every other health food site. One self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only, no external images or scripts.
rubric: The page has one clearly dominant color that the eye associates with the brand, rather than several colors of equal weight competing.
The palette is not the stock health-food default of plain leaf green on white; the choice reads as deliberate for seaweed snacks.
Backgrounds and text neutrals are tinted or chosen on purpose, not pure #000 on pure #fff or a flat default gray.
The Shop now button and any accent color are used sparingly, so the accent stands out instead of appearing on every element.
All text, including text on cards and on the button, is easy to read against its background in the screenshot.
The three product cards are told apart by something restrained (a label, a small swatch) rather than three loud unrelated colors.

prompt:
We're launching Pawline, a telehealth app for pet owners to video-chat with a vet. I want it to feel warm and friendly but the whole thing just looks muddy and tired to me and I can't say why. These are the colors we have right now:

Primary buttons: #8a7f5c
Secondary buttons: #7d8a6b
Highlight / links: #9c8b5e
Page background: #cfc8b0
Body text: #a39b82
Error messages: #b5654a

What's going wrong?
rubric: Identifies that the body text color is far too close in lightness to the background and will be hard to read, and says so directly rather than only calling the palette 'dull'.
Notices that the primary, secondary and highlight colors are all similar in lightness and muted in saturation, so nothing leads and buttons do not stand out from the page.
Explains the muddiness in terms of what is visibly wrong with these specific values (low saturation, similar mid tones, no light-to-dark range), not generic color advice.
Proposes concrete replacement values or direction for at least the text, background and primary action, while keeping the warm, friendly intent.
Does not state contrast numbers that are clearly wrong; if ratios are quoted, the text-on-background figure is shown to be very low.
Ranks the problems or says which fix to make first, and stays proportionate rather than telling them to start over entirely.

prompt: Fernhollow Credit Union is a member-owned credit union in a mid-size town. Its homepage has: a hero with a Join today button, a strip of current loan and savings rates, three calculator tiles, a row of member testimonials, and a dark footer with branch hours. I'm torn between a deep forest green, a navy, and a plum for the main color. Pick one and tell me where color should and shouldn't show up across those sections.
rubric: Commits to one main color instead of hedging among the three, and gives a reason tied to a member-owned, local, trust-oriented institution.
Gives actual hex values (or near equivalents) for the lead color and the supporting neutrals rather than only naming colors.
Says where the lead color appears section by section (for example hero, button, rate strip, footer) and where it stays out, instead of coloring everything.
Names a single action color or treatment for the Join today button and keeps other buttons and links visibly lower in emphasis.
Covers the dark footer and the testimonials with specific color guidance, including legible text on the dark or colored areas.
Notes at least one practical check or risk, such as contrast of text on the lead color or accent colors competing with the main one.
Both a light panel and a dark panel are visible, showing the same episode list, so the comparison is possible from the screenshot.
The dark panel is not a straight inversion or pure black with pure white text; backgrounds and text are softened and the page still looks related to the warm light theme.
Cards or episode rows in the dark panel are visibly separated from the page background by a lighter surface or subtle border, not by heavy shadows.
The orange-red accent is adjusted for the dark background (for example lighter or less saturated) so the play buttons are visible without glowing harshly.
Muted secondary text in the dark panel remains readable, not faded into the background.
The accent is used for the play buttons and at most a few other touches in both panels.

prompt:
I run Quillmark, a one-person letterpress stationery studio. This is the palette for my site and printed price list:

Ink (text and headings): #1f2a2e
Paper (background): #f6f1e7
Rust (links, buttons, my one accent): #b4472a
Sage (small decorative rules and tags): #7c9082
Muted (captions, secondary text): #5f6b6e

A friend said it could feel more premium and polished. Anything you'd change?
rubric: Recognizes that the palette already works (restrained, one clear accent, readable text) and says so plainly instead of inventing problems.
Leaves most or all of the five values unchanged; any suggested change is small and specific (a single value, or a usage note) rather than a new palette.
Does not add gradients, extra accent colors, metallic or gold tones, or a larger set of colors in the name of 'premium'.
Gives a reason for what to keep, for example that the single rust accent on warm paper is what makes it feel crafted.
Any additional advice points at where premium feel actually comes from beyond color changes, briefly, without turning into a long redesign.
The answer is proportionate: short and decisive, not a long list of tweaks.

prompt: I own a bakery called Marrow & Moss. Our website uses a bright orange, #ff6a1a, and it looks great. We just got the printed menu proof back and the same orange came out dull and kind of brownish. The printer says it's 'just how print works' but that feels like a cop-out. Is it? What should I do so the menu looks right?
rubric: Explains in plain language that screens mix light and can show very saturated colors that ordinary ink printing cannot reproduce, so the printer is partly right.
Does not simply side with the printer: distinguishes the unavoidable gamut limit from things the bakery can control, such as specifying the color properly.
Gives practical next steps, such as picking a printable orange (or a spot ink / color-matching reference) and approving a physical proof against it.
Is honest that an exact match to the screen color is not guaranteed and sets expectations about a close, slightly less vivid result.
Mentions that paper stock or coating also changes how the color looks, or that a screen preview of a print file is not a reliable judge.
Is written so a bakery owner with no design background can follow it, without piling on jargon.

prompt: Make the hero section for the Lantern Row Night Market website. Big title, the dates (Friday to Sunday, October 17 to 19), a line like 'Food, crafts and live music after dark', and a Get tickets button. We don't have the photo yet, so fake a dusk sky with CSS gradients for now and put the text right over it. One self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts, no external assets.
rubric: The title, dates and tagline are clearly legible over the gradient across their whole extent, not just where the background happens to be dark.
The Get tickets button is readable and visibly stands out from the sky background.
The dusk gradient moves smoothly between a small number of related hues, without a muddy gray-brown band in the middle or harsh stripes.
The page uses a restrained set of colors, so that the warm accent for the button and lantern-like highlights does not compete with the sky.
Text legibility is achieved by sensible design (a dark enough sky behind light text, or a subtle scrim) rather than by heavy outlines or boxes around every line.
The hero reads as nighttime and festive as a whole at first glance.

prompt: We're designing the dashboard for Quenby Deploy, a tool that shows whether code deployments succeeded. Our brand color is a strong red, #d93a35, and our main buttons use it. I need color for deployment statuses: running, succeeded, failed, and waiting for approval. I was going to be creative and pull the status colors from our brand palette so it all feels on-brand. Good idea?
rubric: Advises against making statuses purely 'on-brand' and recommends keeping the familiar meanings (green for success, a red for failure, amber or yellow for waiting), with a reason.

Spots the conflict that the brand red is also the primary button color and would read as failure or danger, and offers a way to separate them (a different failure shade, a non-red primary, or a clear usage rule).
Gives a specific color for each of the four statuses, with running distinguished from the others (for example blue or neutral).
States that color should not be the only signal and adds a label, icon or shape to each status, with a short reason.
Checks or mentions that text or icons on the status colors stay readable.
Answers the 'good idea?' question directly and does not lecture at length.

prompt: My brand color is a teal, #0f7c80. What neutral should I pair it with for page backgrounds and body text? Two sentences max, no lists, I'm in a hurry.
rubric: The answer is two sentences or fewer and contains no list, bullets or headings.
Gives specific values for at least a background neutral and a text neutral, in hex or an equally precise form.
The suggested neutrals are a defensible partner for the teal (for example slightly warm or slightly teal-tinted rather than a stray hue).
Includes a very brief reason for the choice rather than just the values.
Does not add preamble, caveats or an offer to elaborate that pushes the answer past the limit.

prompt:
Turn these into CSS custom properties I can paste on :root. Name them by what they're for, not what color they are.

#14213d  page headings
#fcfbf8  page background
#ffffff  card background
#3a4660  body text
#0b6e4f  primary button
#c2410c  error text and borders

Thanks.
rubric: Outputs a usable :root block containing all six custom properties.
Every hex value is preserved exactly as given, with none adjusted, substituted or 'improved'.
The names describe the role (for example text, background, surface, action, danger) and not the color itself.
Does not critique the palette or propose different colors; any note is at most one short line.
The response is brief and delivers the code first.
